name: Shimei son of Gera
charge: Cursing the king and casting stones at him
summary: As David fled Jerusalem, Shimei of Saul's house came out cursing and throwing stones and dust: come out, thou bloody man, thou man of Belial. David forbade Abishai to kill him and later swore he would not put him to death. Solomon inherited the case.
offense: As David fled from Absalom, Shimei came out cursing, casting stones, and calling him a bloody man. He claimed that the Lord had returned the blood of Saul's house upon David (2 Samuel 16:5-8). David had repeatedly refused to kill Saul and had judged men who expected reward for deaths within Saul's house. Shimei used David's present distress as proof of an accusation the record did not sustain. Abishai asked leave to take his head, but David restrained him. With his own son seeking his life, David would not make Shimei's abuse the occasion for another immediate killing. He left room for the Lord to look upon his affliction and return good for the cursing (2 Samuel 16:9-12). The restraint belonged to David; it did not turn the curse into lawful speech. Exodus 22:28 forbids cursing the ruler of the people.
judgment: Solomon confined him to Jerusalem on pain of death. Three years later Shimei went to Gath after runaway servants, and Solomon had Benaiah kill him: the Lord shall return thy wickedness upon thine own head.

He claimed that the Lord had returned the blood of Saul's house upon David (2 Samuel 16:5-8). David had repeatedly refused to kill Saul and had judged men who expected reward for deaths within Saul's house. Shimei used David's present distress as proof of an accusation the record did not sustain.

Abishai asked leave to take his head, but David restrained him. With his own son seeking his life, David would not make Shimei's abuse the occasion for another immediate killing. He left room for the Lord to look upon his affliction and return good for the cursing (2 Samuel 16:9-12). The restraint belonged to David; it did not turn the curse into lawful speech. Exodus 22:28 forbids cursing the ruler of the people.

entries.commentary: When David was past the top of the hill, Ziba the servant of Mephibosheth met him with saddled asses, two hundred loaves of bread, a hundred bunches of raisins, a hundred summer fruits, and a bottle of wine. When David asked where his master's son was, Ziba said Mephibosheth abode in Jerusalem, saying the house of Israel would restore him the kingdom of his father. So David gave Ziba all that pertained to Mephibosheth. Ziba came with gifts, and when David asked about Mephibosheth, Ziba claimed Mephibosheth thought the kingdom was about to be restored to him, which was not true. On that word David handed Ziba everything that belonged to Mephibosheth.

As David came to Bahurim, a man of the house of Saul named Shimei the son of Gera came out, cursing and casting stones at David and all his servants. Shimei cursed, calling David a bloody man and a man of Belial, saying the Most High had returned upon him all the blood of the house of Saul, and delivered the kingdom into the hand of Absalom his son, and taken him in his mischief because he was a bloody man. Shimei was of the house of Saul, and Saul was the wicked one who tried to kill David; it was by the hand of the Most High that Saul did not succeed. Yet Shimei cursed David as if David were in the wrong, because word gets around, people gossip and blame, and he saw David at a low state and went to rub it in his face. That is the mindset of some people in Israel as well.

Abishai the son of Zeruiah asked why this dead dog should curse the king, and offered to go take off his head. But the king said, What have I to do with you, ye sons of Zeruiah? Let him curse, because the Most High hath said unto him, Curse David; who shall then say, Wherefore hast thou done so? David rolled with mighty men of war, so Abishai was ready to take Shimei's head off his shoulders. But David said to let him curse, for if it was of the Most High, then let him do it. Just as the Most High brings people to our forums and classrooms who bicker and try to bring confusion, it is of the Most High, sometimes to test the patience of those who pray for patience.

David said to Abishai and all his servants, Behold, my own son who came forth out of my bowels seeketh my life, how much more now may this Benjamite do it? Let him alone and let him curse, for the Most High hath bidden him. It may be that the Most High will look on his affliction and requite him good for the cursing this day. David reasoned that if his own son sought his life, this Benjamite was nothing; the Most High was doing this, so let him curse. It may be the Most High will look on all that was done to David and bless him in front of them, the same as when people try to bring us down and the Most High blesses us before them, which is why this congregation has grown exponentially.

David and his men went by the way while Shimei went along the hillside cursing, throwing stones, and casting dust; and they came weary and refreshed themselves. Absalom and all the men of Israel came to Jerusalem, and Ahithophel with him. When Hushai the Archite, David's friend, came to Absalom saying, God save the king, Absalom asked why he went not with his friend, and Hushai answered that he would serve whom the Most High and Israel chose, and would serve in the presence of the son as he served the father. Hushai put into action the plan he and David made. Absalom challenged him, asking, Is this thy kindness to thy friend? Why wentest thou not with thy friend? This is a real friend, not a friendish one; a true friend tells you when you are wrong and full of it, not the one who only strokes your head and pats your back like Absalom did to steal the people's hearts.

Absalom asked Ahithophel for counsel, and Ahithophel said, Go in unto thy father's concubines whom he left to keep the house, and all Israel shall hear that thou art abhorred of thy father, and the hands of all with thee shall be strong. So they spread Absalom a tent on the top of the house, and Absalom went in unto his father's concubines in the sight of all Israel. The counsel of Ahithophel was as if a man had inquired at the oracle of God. Ahithophel counselled Absalom to lie with the ten concubines David left, in the sight of all Israel, on the roof of the house. This is the exact fulfillment of what the Most High spoke in chapter 12, that David's wives would be taken and one would lie with them in the sight of the sun, and that what David did secretly would be done before all Israel. It was not coincidence or irony; it was prophesied to happen, and none of it would have happened if David had not done what he did. The Most High keeps mercy and forgives, but by no means clears the guilty, so even when we come in and repent, we still must remember the fear of the Most High, for there is but one step between us and death.

The victory that day was turned into mourning for all the people, because they heard how the king grieved for his son, and they got them by stealth into the city as ashamed men steal away when they flee in battle. Joab came into the house and told David he had shamed the faces of all his servants who had saved his life and the lives of his sons, daughters, wives, and concubines, because he loved his enemies and hated his friends. Joab said if Absalom had lived and all of them had died, it would have pleased David well. No one else could speak to the king this way, but Joab knew David's skeletons. Joab charged David to arise and speak comfortably unto his servants, swearing that if he did not, not one man would tarry with him that night, and that would be worse than all the evil that had befallen him from his youth. Then the king arose and sat in the gate, and all the people came before him.

All the tribes of Israel were at strife, saying the king had saved them from the Philistines and their enemies but had fled the land because of Absalom, who was now dead, so why did they say nothing about bringing the king back. David sent to Zadok and Abiathar the priests to speak to the elders of Judah, asking why they were the last to bring the king back when they were his brethren, his bone and his flesh. He told Amasa that he would make him captain of the host in the room of Joab. David bowed the heart of all the men of Judah as the heart of one man, so they sent word for him to return with all his servants, and the king came again to Jordan while Judah came to Gilgal to meet him and conduct him over.

Shimei the son of Gera the Benjamite hastened down with a thousand men of Benjamin, along with Ziba the servant of Saul's house with his sons and servants, and fell down before the king at Jordan. Shimei begged the king not to impute iniquity unto him nor remember the day he did perversely when David went out of Jerusalem, confessing that he had sinned. This was the same Shimei who had cursed David, cast stones, and called him a bloody man and a man of Belial while David was in a low state surrounded by his mighty men. Abishai and the sons of Zeruiah said Shimei should be put to death for cursing the Lord's anointed, but David rebuked them as adversaries, asking whether any man should be put to death that day in Israel when he knew he was king. He swore Shimei would not die. David understood grace long before the New Testament, for grace has always been around.

Mephibosheth the son of Saul came down to meet the king, having neither dressed his feet, trimmed his beard, nor washed his clothes from the day the king departed until he returned in peace, showing his mourning for David. When asked why he had not gone with the king, Mephibosheth said his servant Ziba had deceived him and slandered him, since Mephibosheth was lame and could not saddle his own beast. He acknowledged that all his father's house were dead men before the king, yet David had set him to eat at his own table, so he had no further right to cry to the king. David told him to speak no more of the matter and said that he and Ziba should divide the land. Mephibosheth answered that Ziba could take it all, for it was enough that his lord the king had come again in peace to his own house.

Barzillai the Gileadite, a very aged man of fourscore years, came down from Rogelim to conduct the king over Jordan, having provided the king with sustenance at Mahanaim, for he was a very great man. When David invited him to come and be fed in Jerusalem, Barzillai asked how long he had to live that he should go up, saying at eighty years old he could no longer discern the taste of what he ate or drank nor hear the voice of singing men and women, so he would only go a little way over and asked to return and die in his own city by his parents' grave. He sent Chimham in his place, and the king kissed and blessed Barzillai, who returned to his own place. A quarrel then arose between the men of Israel and the men of Judah over who had the right to bring the king back. Judah claimed the king was near of kin to them, being of the tribe of Judah, while Israel claimed ten parts in the king and more right in David, and the words of Judah were fiercer than the words of Israel. This was the tribe strife that would later split the northern and southern kingdoms, though they were all Israel.

The days of David draw near that he should die, and he charges Solomon to be strong, to keep the charge of the Lord his God, to walk in his ways, and to keep his statutes, commandments, and judgments as written in the law of Moses, that he may prosper. There was a stipulation for the throne to continue: if his children take heed to their way and walk before the Most High in truth with all their heart, the throne stands. Reading through the kings, we see many who broke the commandments, and among their children some were righteous and some unrighteous. -
Solomon thrusts out Abiathar from being priest unto the Lord, fulfilling the word the Most High spoke concerning the house of Eli in Shiloh. The old judgment on Eli's line is carried out.

Joab, who had turned after Adonijah, flees to the tabernacle of the Lord and catches hold of the horns of the altar, but Solomon sends Benaiah to fall upon him. Joab dies for the innocent blood he shed when he slew Abner and Amasa, two men more righteous and better than he, without David's knowledge. The blood returns upon Joab's own head and upon his seed, while upon David and his seed and throne there shall be peace forever from the Lord. Benaiah is set over the host in his place.

Shimei is commanded to build a house in Jerusalem and dwell there, never crossing the brook Kidron on pain of death, and he agrees. After three years he goes to Gath after his runaway servants and breaks the oath, so Solomon has Benaiah put him to death, and the kingdom is established in Solomon's hand.

If a man steal an ox or a sheep and kill it or sell it, he restores five oxen for an ox and four sheep for a sheep. We are in a different situation where we do not keep oxen and sheep, but the principle of restitution still applies among brothers and sisters in the body: if something is stolen, the law written here governs the payback. Do not be stealing.

If a thief be found breaking up means breaking in. He entered your home and you defended yourself and he died: that is what is called self-defense today, and no blood is shed for him, meaning there is no judgment. The judgment was already passed in the breaking in. If the sun be risen upon him, the thief got away, and there shall be blood shed for him means there shall be a judgment; then the verse gives the judgment. He makes full restitution, and if he have nothing he is sold for his theft: not sold into slavery, but into work servitude until he pays off the debt of what he stole. If the theft be found in his hand alive, he restores double. Verse three covers the thief who already got rid of what he stole; verse four covers the one still holding it.

These are self-explanatory: if a man lets his beast feed in another man's field or vineyard, he makes restitution of the best of his own field and vineyard; and he that kindles a fire that consumes another man's corn surely makes restitution.

If a man deliver money or stuff to his neighbor to keep and it be stolen, the thief found pays double. If the thief be not found, the master of the house is brought unto the judges, to see whether he put his hand unto his neighbor's goods, whether he was part of a scheme to deceive the owner out of his goods. For all manner of trespass, whether for ox, ass, sheep, raiment, or any lost thing, both parties come before the judges, and whom the judges condemn pays double unto his neighbor.

If a beast delivered to a neighbor to keep die or be hurt or driven away, no man seeing it, an oath of the Lord is between them both. In layman's terms he swears: I did not take the stuff, I did not set you up, I do not know where it is. The owner accepts the oath and the matter ends there; it is not to be spoken of again. Paul uses this civil law to show how the Most High is unchangeable. An oath for confirmation is the end of all strife; God confirmed his counsel by an oath, and by two immutable things, that it is impossible for God to lie and that he will not take back what went out of his mouth, we have strong consolation. The same way, once the oath of this law is applied, the matter is over.

If the thing kept be stolen from him, he makes restitution; if it be torn in pieces, he brings it for witness and does not make it good. If a man borrow ought of his neighbor, ought meaning anything, and it be hurt or die with the owner not present, he surely makes it good. You borrowed it, it got messed up, you owe the man. But if the owner be with it, or if it be an hired thing, it came for its hire. If you came to plow a man's field for ten shekels with your own donkey and your donkey breaks his leg, you cannot expect the owner to pay for your own faulty equipment; the same as a business loan today, the property owner is not liable when your own equipment breaks down.

If a man entice a maid that is not betrothed and lie with her, he shall surely endow her to be his wife; he has to sign the papers. He is at fault for not going through the proper channels of marriage, and she is at fault for being enticed and laying down. The proper channel was that the father married off the daughter. To marry thy daughter is to perform a weighty matter, for the father gives her over to that man for the rest of her life and is out of all watching over her; so she is to be given to a man of understanding, one keeping the commandments as a wise man. In our own land the daughter went from her father's house to a husband's house with the blessing of the father.

Thou shalt not suffer a witch to live: witchcraft goes into horoscopes, palm readings, and all things of that nature. Whosoever lieth with a beast, bestiality, shall surely be put to death. He that sacrificeth unto any god save unto the Lord only shall be utterly destroyed.

This is twofold, and first and foremost the stranger is your brother from a different area, our own people. [Leviticus 25](/bible/leviticus/25) shows it: if thy brother be waxen poor, though he be a stranger or a sojourner, sojourn meaning travel, thou shalt relieve him that he may live with thee. A brother of another tribe who falls on hard times and travels down to live with you is that stranger; neither vex him nor oppress him, for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt.

Ye shall not afflict any widow or fatherless child. A wife without a husband already has a hard life, and a son or daughter without a father the same; do not make their life harder than it already is. If thou afflict them in any wise and they cry unto the Most High, he will surely hear their cry, and his wrath shall wax hot: he will kill you with the sword, and your own wives shall be widows and your children fatherless. That is the Lord's plain warning against mistreating those less fortunate.

Usury means interest. You cannot charge your brother or sister interest: if you lend twenty dollars, you get twenty dollars back, nothing more, nothing less; no little bit more off the top. This is the same law read in [Leviticus 25:36-37](/bible/leviticus/25#v36).

If thou take thy neighbor's raiment to pledge, deliver it unto him by that the sun goeth down, for that is his covering only; wherein shall he sleep? The tunics and overcoats worn then were also sleeping garments to keep a man warm at night, especially the poor. A well-off man does not have to work for you; this speaks of the less fortunate who extend their services for money and give what is most valuable to them, their raiment, as the pledge. If he cries unto the Most High, he will hear, for he is gracious.

Thou shalt not revile the gods means do not hate or speak evil of your leaders. The word gods here is the leaders over you: the Most High says in the psalm, I have said, Ye are gods, and all of you are children of the Most High, speaking of us. [Acts 23](/bible/acts/23) is the example: when Paul spoke against the high priest, they that stood by said, Revilest thou God's high priest? And Paul answered, I wist not, brethren, that he was the high priest: for it is written, Thou shalt not speak evil of the ruler of thy people, quoting this very verse.

Thou shalt not delay to offer the first of thy ripe fruits and of thy liquors, and the firstborn of thy sons shalt thou give unto me. The firstborn sons that opened the matrix were consecrated unto the Lord, and the father redeemed them back from the priest with shekels. Likewise with the oxen and the sheep: seven days the firstling stayed with his dam, his mother, and on the eighth day it was given. The Lord did not want it too young, taken as soon as it popped out; it had to be its appointed time with the mother, then brought to the priest.

Ye shall be holy men unto me: neither shall ye eat any flesh that is torn of beasts in the field; ye shall cast it to the dogs. This is twofold, and the dogs are the strangers of other nations, the aliens and foreigners. Always get the context of the law, because sometimes the stranger is your brother and sometimes it is literally the other nations. [Deuteronomy 14:21](/bible/deuteronomy/14#v21) doubles this law: that which dieth of itself thou shalt give unto the stranger that is in thy gates, or sell it unto an alien, for thou art an holy people unto the Lord thy God. Cast the torn flesh to the other nations; ye shall not eat it, because ye are holy people.

Dead flies make the apothecary's ointment stink; so a little folly ruins the man who holds a reputation for wisdom and honor. A wise man's heart is at his right hand, but a fool's heart at his left. Even as the fool walks by the way his wisdom fails him, and he shows everyone that he is a fool. If the spirit of the ruler rises against you, leave not your place, for yielding pacifies great offenses.

There is an evil under the sun, an error that proceeds from the ruler: folly is set in high dignity while the rich sit in a low place. He has seen servants riding upon horses and princes walking as servants upon the earth, the natural order turned upside down.

He that digs a pit shall fall into it, and whoever breaks a hedge a serpent shall bite; he that removes stones is hurt by them, and he that cleaves wood is endangered by it. If the iron is blunt and the edge is not whetted, more strength is needed, but wisdom is profitable to direct. The serpent bites without enchantment, and a babbler is no better.

The words of a wise man's mouth are gracious, but the fool is swallowed up by his own lips. His talk begins in foolishness and ends in mischievous madness. A fool is full of words, though no man can tell what shall be after him. The labor of the foolish wearies every one of them because he does not even know how to go to the city.

Woe to the land whose king is a child and whose princes eat in the morning; blessed is the land whose king is the son of nobles and whose princes eat in due season, for strength and not for drunkenness. Slothfulness lets the building decay and idleness makes the house drop through. A feast is made for laughter and wine makes merry, but money answers all things. Curse not the king, not even in your thought, nor the rich in your bedchamber, for a bird of the air shall carry the voice and tell the matter.

verses.text: And when king David came to Bahurim, behold, thence came out a man of the family of the house of Saul, whose name was Shimei, the son of Gera: he came forth, and cursed still as he came.
And he cast stones at David, and at all the servants of king David: and all the people and all the mighty men were on his right hand and on his left.
And thus said Shimei when he cursed, Come out, come out, thou bloody man, and thou man of Belial:

The Lord hath returned upon thee all the blood of the house of Saul, in whose stead thou hast reigned; and the Lord hath delivered the kingdom into the hand of Absalom thy son: and, behold, thou art taken in thy mischief, because thou art a bloody man.
Then said Abishai the son of Zeruiah unto the king, Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? let me go over, I pray thee, and take off his head.
And the king said, What have I to do with you, ye sons of Zeruiah? so let him curse, because the Lord hath said unto him, Curse David. Who shall then say, Wherefore hast thou done so?

And David said to Abishai, and to all his servants, Behold, my son, which came forth of my bowels, seeketh my life: how much more now may this Benjamite do it? let him alone, and let him curse; for the Lord hath bidden him.
It may be that the Lord will look on mine affliction, and that the Lord will requite me good for his cursing this day.
And as David and his men went by the way, Shimei went along on the hill’s side over against him, and cursed as he went, and threw stones at him, and cast dust.
And there went over a ferry boat to carry over the king’s household, and to do what he thought good. And Shimei the son of Gera fell down before the king, as he was come over Jordan;

And said unto the king, Let not my lord impute iniquity unto me, neither do thou remember that which thy servant did perversely the day that my lord the king went out of Jerusalem, that the king should take it to his heart.
For thy servant doth know that I have sinned: therefore, behold, I am come the first this day of all the house of Joseph to go down to meet my lord the king.
But Abishai the son of Zeruiah answered and said, Shall not Shimei be put to death for this, because he cursed the Lord’s anointed?

And David said, What have I to do with you, ye sons of Zeruiah, that ye should this day be adversaries unto me? shall there any man be put to death this day in Israel? for do not I know that I am this day king over Israel?
Therefore the king said unto Shimei, Thou shalt not die. And the king sware unto him.

And, behold, thou hast with thee Shimei the son of Gera, a Benjamite of Bahurim, which cursed me with a grievous curse in the day when I went to Mahanaim: but he came down to meet me at Jordan, and I sware to him by the Lord, saying, I will not put thee to death with the sword.
Now therefore hold him not guiltless: for thou art a wise man, and knowest what thou oughtest to do unto him; but his hoar head bring thou down to the grave with blood.
And the king sent and called for Shimei, and said unto him, Build thee an house in Jerusalem, and dwell there, and go not forth thence any whither.
For it shall be, that on the day thou goest out, and passest over the brook Kidron, thou shalt know for certain that thou shalt surely die: thy blood shall be upon thine own head.
And Shimei said unto the king, The saying is good: as my lord the king hath said, so will thy servant do. And Shimei dwelt in Jerusalem many days.
And it came to pass at the end of three years, that two of the servants of Shimei ran away unto Achish son of Maachah king of Gath. And they told Shimei, saying, Behold, thy servants be in Gath.
And Shimei arose, and saddled his ass, and went to Gath to Achish to seek his servants: and Shimei went, and brought his servants from Gath.
And it was told Solomon that Shimei had gone from Jerusalem to Gath, and was come again.

And the king sent and called for Shimei, and said unto him, Did I not make thee to swear by the Lord, and protested unto thee, saying, Know for a certain, on the day thou goest out, and walkest abroad any whither, that thou shalt surely die? and thou saidst unto me, The word that I have heard is good.
Why then hast thou not kept the oath of the Lord, and the commandment that I have charged thee with?

The king said moreover to Shimei, Thou knowest all the wickedness which thine heart is privy to, that thou didst to David my father: therefore the Lord shall return thy wickedness upon thine own head;
And king Solomon shall be blessed, and the throne of David shall be established before the Lord for ever.
So the king commanded Benaiah the son of Jehoiada; which went out, and fell upon him, that he died. And the kingdom was established in the hand of Solomon.
Thou shalt not revile the gods, nor curse the ruler of thy people.
Curse not the king, no not in thy thought; and curse not the rich in thy bedchamber: for a bird of the air shall carry the voice, and that which hath wings shall tell the matter.

And as David and his men went by the way, Shimei went along on the hill’s side over against him, and cursed as he went, and threw stones at him, and cast dust.
And there went over a ferry boat to carry over the king’s household, and to do what he thought good. And Shimei the son of Gera fell down before the king, as he was come over Jordan;

And said unto the king, Let not my lord impute iniquity unto me, neither do thou remember that which thy servant did perversely the day that my lord the king went out of Jerusalem, that the king should take it to his heart.
For thy servant doth know that I have sinned: therefore, behold, I am come the first this day of all the house of Joseph to go down to meet my lord the king.
But Abishai the son of Zeruiah answered and said, Shall not Shimei be put to death for this, because he cursed the Lord’s anointed?

And David said, What have I to do with you, ye sons of Zeruiah, that ye should this day be adversaries unto me? shall there any man be put to death this day in Israel? for do not I know that I am this day king over Israel?
Therefore the king said unto Shimei, Thou shalt not die. And the king sware unto him.

And, behold, thou hast with thee Shimei the son of Gera, a Benjamite of Bahurim, which cursed me with a grievous curse in the day when I went to Mahanaim: but he came down to meet me at Jordan, and I sware to him by the Lord, saying, I will not put thee to death with the sword.
Now therefore hold him not guiltless: for thou art a wise man, and knowest what thou oughtest to do unto him; but his hoar head bring thou down to the grave with blood.
And the king sent and called for Shimei, and said unto him, Build thee an house in Jerusalem, and dwell there, and go not forth thence any whither.
For it shall be, that on the day thou goest out, and passest over the brook Kidron, thou shalt know for certain that thou shalt surely die: thy blood shall be upon thine own head.
And Shimei said unto the king, The saying is good: as my lord the king hath said, so will thy servant do. And Shimei dwelt in Jerusalem many days.
And it came to pass at the end of three years, that two of the servants of Shimei ran away unto Achish son of Maachah king of Gath. And they told Shimei, saying, Behold, thy servants be in Gath.
And Shimei arose, and saddled his ass, and went to Gath to Achish to seek his servants: and Shimei went, and brought his servants from Gath.
And it was told Solomon that Shimei had gone from Jerusalem to Gath, and was come again.

And the king sent and called for Shimei, and said unto him, Did I not make thee to swear by the Lord, and protested unto thee, saying, Know for a certain, on the day thou goest out, and walkest abroad any whither, that thou shalt surely die? and thou saidst unto me, The word that I have heard is good.
Why then hast thou not kept the oath of the Lord, and the commandment that I have charged thee with?

The king said moreover to Shimei, Thou knowest all the wickedness which thine heart is privy to, that thou didst to David my father: therefore the Lord shall return thy wickedness upon thine own head;
And king Solomon shall be blessed, and the throne of David shall be established before the Lord for ever.
So the king commanded Benaiah the son of Jehoiada; which went out, and fell upon him, that he died. And the kingdom was established in the hand of Solomon.
Thou shalt not revile the gods, nor curse the ruler of thy people.
Curse not the king, no not in thy thought; and curse not the rich in thy bedchamber: for a bird of the air shall carry the voice, and that which hath wings shall tell the matter.
